Singapore Recalls 2018 Currency Shock as Economy Remains Stable

SINGAPORE, June 13—Singaporean officials and economists this week reflected on the aftermath of the 2018 currency shock that rattled the city-state’s economy and sent tremors through Southeast Asian markets, noting that the country has since regained stability and that economic activity is currently undisturbed.

In June 2018, the Singapore dollar unexpectedly plunged by nearly 12% against the US dollar over the course of two weeks, after speculative trading and capital outflows triggered by tightening US interest rates and emerging-market jitters. The sudden depreciation briefly pushed up import prices, squeezed household budgets, and forced the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to intervene in currency markets.

“Looking back, the 2018 currency shock posed significant challenges for our open economy,” said MAS Deputy Managing Director Elaine Goh during a forum Wednesday. “Swift policy action, including targeted intervention and communication, helped restore confidence and stabilize the Singapore dollar.”

Inflation spiked to 3.6% in July 2018—well above the year’s earlier average of 0.6%—fueling concerns among unions and consumer groups. “Families struggled as everyday items became more expensive,” recalled Tan Wei Ming, president of the Singapore Retail Association. “Retailers had to adapt quickly, sourcing alternatives and absorbing some of the costs.”

Singapore’s export-driven manufacturing sector was also hit as imported components became costlier. “Many firms hedged against currency swings, but the volatility was unprecedented,” said Lee Jun Kai, chief economist at Southeast Asia Markets Institute. “Some smaller exporters suffered losses or delayed shipments.”

The MAS’s intervention, together with a rebound in regional investor sentiment, steadied the currency by late July. By year’s end, the Singapore dollar had recovered most of its losses, and inflation had returned to near its long-term average.

Analysts attribute Singapore’s recovery to prudent reserve management and strong fundamentals. “The episode underscored the importance of transparency and policy credibility,” Lee said.

Today, Singapore’s financial system remains robust, with the MAS reporting stable currency reserves and moderate inflation. No disruptions to economic activity are currently observed. “We have learned from 2018 and are better prepared for future shocks,” Goh said.
